items.title: Hermes Webapp: Run the Full Hermes Desktop in Any Browser
items.content:
The Hermes webapp puts the whole Hermes Desktop workspace in a normal browser tab: your chats, profiles, scheduled jobs, files, Git review and even a terminal. It’s served by the Hermes gateway itself and opened with one command, `hermes webapp`. It’s listed in Hermes v0.22.6, released on 2 November 2026, along with a Web Access pane in the Desktop app to open it from your phone or another computer behind Nous sign-in. Below is how to turn it on, how sign-in works, how to reach it safely from other devices, and how it compares with the Desktop app and older web UIs. My video is right under this intro.

Key takeaways

- Turn on: `hermes config set webapp.enabled true`, restart the gateway, run `hermes webapp`.

- Serves at `http://127.0.0.1:9120` by default and opens a one-use sign-in link.

- Settings → Web Access opens it on your network or your own HTTPS URL, behind Nous sign-in.

- A signed-in user can run commands as you, so never expose it without sign-in.

- Want your AI agents reachable from anywhere, safely? Claim a free strategy session.

## What is the Hermes webapp?

The Hermes Desktop docs describe it as the Desktop workspace served to a browser: sessions, profiles, Capabilities, Messaging, Artifacts, scheduled jobs, the host file tree, Git review, previews and the terminal rail.

Two things make it different from older ways of using Hermes in a browser:

- It’s not the Web Dashboard. It’s the full Desktop experience.

- Chats run on the same gateway that serves the CLI, the native Desktop and your messaging apps, so every surface sees one conversation with one queue.

The gateway serves it from its own listener, and Desktop plugins can now load in a browser tab too.

## How to turn on the Hermes webapp

```
hermes config set webapp.enabled true
hermes gateway restart
hermes webapp
```

`hermes webapp` builds the bundle if it’s out of date (the first build can take a few minutes), starts the gateway if it isn’t running, and opens a sign-in link in your browser. The default address is `http://127.0.0.1:9120`, which you can change with `webapp.host` and `webapp.port`.

Useful options from the CLI reference:

- `hermes webapp --status`: is the gateway serving it, and at which address.

- `hermes webapp --no-open`: print the link instead of opening a browser.

- `hermes webapp --sign-out`: sign out every browser tab at once.

- `hermes -p work webapp`: open it on a named profile.

Easier option: ask your agent, “Turn on the Hermes webapp, restart the gateway and give me the status.”

## How sign-in works

On your own machine there’s no password. Instead:

- The link works once, within 60 seconds. The browser swaps it for a sign-in that stays in that tab, so reloads and gateway restarts keep you signed in.

- A fresh tab or a bare URL shows instructions, not access. Run `hermes webapp` again for a new link.

- New windows and pop-outs get their own one-use link.

- On Linux the gateway checks the browser connection belongs to your user. On macOS the link is written to a page only your user can read.

If a link is printed for you to open (over SSH, for example), keep it private: until it’s used, it signs a browser in as you.

## Open it from your phone or another computer

In the native Desktop app, Settings → Web Access turns the webapp on for other devices, behind sign-in with your Nous account. Only the native app can change this setting; a browser signed in over the network can’t.

- This network: devices on the same Wi-Fi open `http://<this computer’s address>:9120`. It’s plain HTTP, so only use it on a network you trust.

- My own URL: an HTTPS address you already run, such as Tailscale Serve, a tunnel or a reverse proxy, forwarding to `127.0.0.1`. It’s saved as `webapp.public_url`.

Start builds the webapp, registers its sign-in with your Nous account, saves the settings and restarts the gateway. If a chat is running, it waits and shows Restart needed. The docs are clear on one thing: never forward the port from your router directly.

## Safety: treat it like access to your computer

The docs put this in a warning box, and it’s the most important line on this page: a signed-in webapp user can run any command as the account running Hermes, use agent tools, read host files and Git, and reach that account’s credentials.

- Never expose it without a sign-in provider. Setting `webapp.host` to `0.0.0.0` requires the dashboard sign-in gate.

- Use a username and password only on a trusted LAN or VPN; use OAuth/OIDC for anything internet-facing.

- Prefer an SSH tunnel, Tailscale or another trusted VPN, and HTTPS for remote use.

- Over plain HTTP on another device, browsers switch off the bot screen viewer, the microphone, clipboard reading and notifications. HTTPS or an SSH tunnel keeps them.

Older chats written before the gateway owned sessions can be read in the browser but not continued until you run `hermes sessions adopt` once on the host. For other browser options, see my Hermes Agent web UI and Hermes Agent dashboard guides.

## The webapp terminal

The terminal rail opens the host’s shell in your home folder. Drop files on it to upload them (16 MiB each). Refreshing the page detaches the terminal without ending it, and it reattaches when you come back.

Detached shells are kept for 15 minutes while the gateway runs, with up to 16 host terminals in total. A gateway restart or update ends them.

## My verdict

If you want to check on your agents from a laptop, a tablet or your phone, this is now the cleanest way. Turn it on locally first, then use Web Access with your own HTTPS address or Tailscale, and never open it to the internet without sign-in. That’s the safe way to use the Hermes webapp.

Run hermes config set webapp.enabled true, restart the gateway with hermes gateway restart, then run hermes webapp. It opens a one-use sign-in link at http://127.0.0.1:9120 by default.

Yes. In the native Desktop app open Settings, Web Access and choose This network or My own URL. Devices then sign in with your Nous account.

Only behind a sign-in provider and ideally HTTPS, an SSH tunnel or a VPN such as Tailscale. A signed-in user can run commands as the account running Hermes, so never forward the port from your router.

No. The Web Dashboard is a separate tool. The webapp is the full Desktop workspace in a browser, running on the same gateway as the CLI, Desktop and messaging.

items.title: Hermes Vault: Let Your Agent Log In Without Seeing Your Passwords
items.content:
The Hermes vault is how Hermes Agent signs into websites, enters two-factor codes and fills your address or card at checkout without the model ever seeing a password. Say “log into GitHub” and, the first time, Hermes asks you for the login in a masked prompt. After that it just works. The newest change landed in Hermes v0.22.6 on 2 November 2026: you can now keep the vault’s encryption key in your computer’s own keychain instead of a file. Below is what the vault stores, the commands, password manager support, the keychain option and the limits to know. My video is right under this intro.

Key takeaways

- Saves logins, 2FA keys, cards and addresses, each bound to one website.

- The model never sees passwords: Hermes fills them straight into the page.

- Commands: `hermes vault list`, `add`, `rm`, `sources` and `key`.

- New in v0.22.6: an opt-in OS keychain home for the vault key.

- Want AI agents handling logins for your business safely? Claim a free strategy session.

## What does the Hermes vault store?

The Passwords & Logins docs describe four kinds of item, all encrypted on your machine under `~/.hermes/vault/` and kept per profile:

- Website logins: your username or email plus the password, tied to the exact site (for example `https://github.com`).

- Two-factor setup keys: the “setup key” or `otpauth://` link a site shows when you turn on 2FA. Hermes then generates the code itself, and the item shows a 2FA auto badge.

- Cards for checkout pages.

- Addresses for shipping and billing forms.

Labels, site addresses and usernames are visible metadata. Passwords and card numbers never leave the vault except into the page they belong to.

## How the vault keeps passwords away from the model

When Hermes fills a password, the tool result the model sees is just a note like `{filled_fields: 1, origin: "https://github.com"}`. The docs list what that means:

- The password never enters the model’s context through Hermes: not tool results, logs, the session database or any command line.

- A fill is refused unless the page address exactly matches the saved site, checked again inside the page right before writing.

- The password is also registered with the redactor, so a later page read can’t echo it back.

- Codes sent to your phone or email are typed into a small prompt by you and entered by Hermes; they never enter the chat either.

- For passkeys, hardware keys and app approvals (“tap Approve in Duo”), Hermes tells you to finish on your device and waits.

## Add and manage logins

Most people never run a command: the first time the agent hits a sign-in page with no saved login, it asks you on the spot. In Hermes Desktop you see a “Save your github.com login?” card with Save & sign in or Don’t save.

To manage things yourself, use Desktop → Settings → Passwords & Logins, or the CLI:

```
hermes vault list
hermes vault add
hermes vault rm <handle>
hermes vault sources
hermes vault key
```

Easier option: ask your agent, “Show me what’s saved in my Hermes vault and remove any login I haven’t used for a site I no longer need.”

## Use 1Password or Bitwarden with Hermes

Nothing to switch on. If the `op` or `bw` command-line tool is installed and signed in, Hermes picks it up and those website logins become fillable next to the local ones.

- The first time a manager login is needed, Hermes asks for your master password in a masked prompt, once per session, locking again after 30 minutes idle.

- Hermes keeps only the session token in memory, never the master password.

- An item listing several websites fills on each of those exact addresses and nothing else.

- Opt out with `hermes vault sources --disable bitwarden` or the switch in Settings.

For unattended jobs, the docs suggest a 1Password service account token (`OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`), because a locked manager can’t be unlocked when nobody is there.

## Cards and addresses: what needs your OK

Cards and addresses are saved once and filled only on their checkout site. The safety rule that matters most for a business:

- Every card fill asks you first, with the same approval prompt as a dangerous command. Declining writes nothing.

## New: keep the vault key in your OS keychain

By default the encryption key sits in `~/.hermes/vault/vault.key` next to the encrypted vault. v0.22.6 adds an opt-in move to the macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or Secret Service / KWallet on Linux:

```

hermes vault key migrate --to keychain    # move it into the keychain
hermes vault key migrate --to file        # move it back
```

The move copies the key, checks the keychain copy opens your vault, and only then deletes the file, so an interrupted move still leaves a working vault. It also sets `vault.key_storage` for new vaults.

Why bother: with the default file, anyone holding a backup or synced copy of `~/.hermes` can decrypt the vault because the key travels with it. With keychain storage, a backup holds only scrambled data.

The docs explain why it’s opt-in rather than the default:

- A lost entry means lost items. Delete the keychain entry and the vault can’t be opened; Hermes says so rather than creating a new key over it.

- On a headless Linux server with no keyring, a new vault’s key falls back to the file with a warning.

One limit applies in both modes: a plugin running inside Hermes can do anything Hermes can, including filling a saved login. If you save logins and install plugins you haven’t reviewed, the docs recommend running plugins out of process with `plugins.isolation: host`.

items.title: What We Keep of What We Forget: Replacement Operators and Routing Semantics in Training-Free MoE Expert Pruning
items.content: Training-free expert pruning makes two decisions: which experts to remove, and what the layer computes when its router still selects a removed expert. Published methods change both at once. Holding the mask fixed, we compare replacement operators from three families on OLMoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight, with Granite as a fourth router, using paired, multiplicity-corrected tests. The largest effect is a choice usually left implicit: the survivors' gate scale. On routers trained without top-k

items.title: Grok Bot Free Trial: How It Works and How to Cancel It
items.content:
Is there a Grok Bot free trial? For some accounts, yes, but it works differently from most app trials. Per the official FAQ, the trial is a usage credit with a 7-day window, and it never turns into a paid plan. The App Store trial on iPhone is a separate thing that Apple runs, and Android has no in-app trial at all. The 27 October changelog also changed what some screens show. Below is exactly how each one works, how to make the credit last, how to cancel, and the new template that handles free trials of other services for you. My video is right under this intro.

Key takeaways

- Some accounts see Start Trial on the access screen: a usage credit plus a 7-day window.

- It never turns into a paid plan, and used credit isn’t restored.

- An App Store trial is Apple’s, and it converts to paid unless you cancel first.

- Android has no in-app trial.

## Is there a Grok Bot free trial?

The FAQ answer: some accounts can try Grok Bot before they pay. When the access screen offers Start Trial, choose it. Not every account gets the offer.

The v0.78.1 changelog (27 October 2026) adds a change: where Grok Bot used to offer a free trial, it now offers Get Grok Bot with a unified plan and See Unified Plans. So if you don’t see Start Trial, that’s why.

Grok Bot also isn’t a separate subscription. The Get started docs say it’s included with Premium, Super and Ultra on The X Subscription and with paid legacy Cursor plans, and you can link an individual SuperGrok or X Premium+ subscription. Check the current plans on the official pages; I don’t quote prices here.

## How the usage-credit trial works

- The trial is a usage credit, and a 7-day window also applies.

- It never turns into a paid plan, so there’s no surprise charge from the trial itself.

- The credit is used up by how much work your agents do, measured by agent steps and tokens, not by how many messages you send.

- One big task can use all of it, and used credit isn’t restored.

Grok (the chat app) and Grok Bot are two different apps, so a SuperGrok paywall or weekly limit in the Grok app is not about Grok Bot.

## How to make the trial credit last

The FAQ’s advice is to start small, scope tasks tightly and check usage before big jobs. In practice:

- Give the Bot one clear, small task first, such as summarising one inbox label, not “clean up my whole business”.

- Check your usage on the plan screen before anything long-running.

- Save a working task as a skill instead of re-explaining it; see Grok Bot skills.

- Leave big scheduled routines until you’re on a plan.

## How to cancel the Grok Bot free trial

Cancel Trial appears on free-plan accounts, and there’s no charge to cancel:

- Desktop: Settings → Usage & Billing → Cancel Trial.

- iPhone and Android: Settings → Usage → Cancel Trial.

- Cancelling removes any remaining trial credit, and you can’t start the trial again.

- On a paid plan or a Teams seat, the trial ends on its own.

## App Store and Android trials

Phone trials follow the store’s rules, per the mobile docs:

- iPhone: an App Store free trial (intro offer) is run by Apple and turns into a paid Apple subscription unless you cancel first. Cancel in Apple ID → Subscriptions before it ends.

- Android: there is no in-app trial. Google Play handles in-app subscriptions under Payments & subscriptions.

- Only monthly individual plans are sold in the mobile app, and Cursor can’t cancel or refund an in-app plan for you.

- If you already have access from a plan or a SuperGrok link, don’t buy a second subscription in the app.
